text: You could count every cookie.
That works. But it's slow, and it's easy to lose your place.
Is there a faster way? Yes. Look at the plates.
When every group has the same number, you can count a whole group at a time.
Look. Each plate is a group.
There are four plates, so there are four groups.
And each plate has three cookies. That's three in each group.
Now count one whole plate at a time.
three, six, nine, twelve.
So there are twelve cookies.
four groups of three make twelve.
We write that as four times three equals twelve.
The first number is the groups. The second is how many in each.
Here's the part people mix up.

text: When chairs are jumbled, you have to count every one.
And it's easy to miss some.
What if they stand in neat rows? Then it's much faster.
When every row has the same number, count the rows, count one row, then multiply.
Look. Rows go across, from left to right.
Count them. one, two, three.
There are three rows.
Every row is the same, so you only need to count one.
one, two, three, four, five.

text: Each row has five chairs.
Now count one whole row at a time. five, ten, fifteen.
three rows of five is fifteen.
We write it as three times five equals fifteen.
If one row is missing a chair, it is not three times five any more.
Every row must have the same number. Count each row to check.
Turn the tray, and now there are five rows of two.
It looks different. So did the number of muffins change?
Turning the rows around does not change how many there are, so two times five and five times two make the same total.
First, the tray as it started. two rows of five.
Count by rows. five, ten.
So two times five equals ten.
Now watch the tray turn.
Does any muffin fall off? No. Is any muffin added? No.
Every muffin just moves to a new spot.
Now count the turned tray by rows. two, four, six, eight, ten.
So five times two equals ten.
Same muffins, same total.
This turn-around trick works for times. It does not work for take away.
five minus two leaves three. But two minus five does not leave three, so they are not the same.
You could count every sock, one at a time.
But socks come in pairs. Is there a faster way? Yes.
When the groups are the same size, jump by that size, and each jump counts a whole group.
Look at the number line. Each pair is one jump of two.
two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve.
How many jumps did we make? Count them. six jumps of two.
And we landed on twelve.
So six times two equals twelve.
fives work the same way. Each hand is a jump of five. five, ten, fifteen.
And bundles of ten jump by tens. ten, twenty, thirty, forty.
four hands means four jumps. Don't stop at fifteen.
Hold up a finger for each jump. five, ten, fifteen, twenty.
You already count by twos, fives and tens.
Counting by threes is new, so it doesn't come as easily yet.
Can you do it the same way? Yes.
threes and fours work just like twos and fives, so add the same number every time you jump.
Each tricycle has three wheels, so each is a jump of three.
Three, six, nine, twelve.
four jumps of three make twelve.
A car has four wheels. Jump by fours.
Four, eight, twelve.
three jumps of four make twelve.
Now write them down.
four tricycles have twelve wheels, so four times three equals twelve.
three cars have twelve wheels, so three times four equals twelve.
Counting by threes does not mean add one each time.
That gives three, four, five, six. Every jump adds a whole group of three, so it goes three, six, nine, twelve.
What does fair mean here?
If one friend gets six and another gets two, that isn't fair.
Every friend must get the same number.
Division shares a total into equal groups, and here we know how many groups, so we find how many in each.
Give one apple to each friend. That is one round.
Then go round again. Now each friend has two.
Keep going, round and round, until the basket is empty.
Now count the first friend's apples. One, two, three, four.
Each friend has four apples, and it is fair.
twelve shared by three friends is four each.
We write twelve divided by three equals four.

Find six hours along the bottom. Is there a dot to read?
No. Nobody in this class studied that long.
And a guess is not a plan, so we need the line itself.
The line is a rule, so put the x value into its equation and the y value you get is your prediction.
Where does the line start, at zero hours? At fifty.
From there it climbs five points for every hour.
So its equation is y equals five x plus fifty.
Maya studies six hours, so six goes in for x.
five times six is thirty. Then thirty plus fifty is eighty.
So we predict a score of eighty for her.
What do the two numbers mean?
The five means about five more points for every extra hour.
The fifty is where the line starts, the score at zero hours.
Don't stop at five times six. That thirty is only the extra points from studying.
Add the fifty the line starts at, and you get eighty.
Here is what we know so far.
twenty-seven students like pizza, and twenty students are in grade seven.
So how many grade seven students like pizza? Those two counts cannot tell you.
Put one question in the rows and one in the columns, so each box counts the people who fit both.
Let's fill one box together.
twelve students are in grade seven and they like pizza.
Where does that twelve go? Right where the Grade seven row meets the Likes pizza column.
Now check each row. It has to add up to its own total.
In grade seven, twelve and eight make twenty.
In grade eight, fifteen and five make twenty as well.
Does it work going down, too? Yes.
Down the Likes pizza column, twelve and fifteen make twenty-seven.
Down the Does not column, eight and five make thirteen.
And twenty-seven and thirteen make forty, the same forty you get from twenty and twenty.
Don't add a row total to a column total.
The twelve grade seven pizza fans are in both, so they get counted twice.
Add the two row totals instead. twenty and twenty make all forty.
fifteen is more than twelve, sure. But look at the row totals.
Grade eight has thirty students, and grade seven has only twenty.
So is fifteen out of thirty really more than twelve out of twenty? The counts alone cannot tell us.
Divide each count by the total of its own group, and then groups of different sizes compare fairly.
Start with grade seven. twelve of their twenty students like pizza.
Divide twelve by twenty and you get zero point six.
That is sixty out of every one hundred, so sixty percent.
Now grade eight. fifteen of their thirty students like pizza.
Divide fifteen by thirty and you get zero point five, or fifty percent.
So which grade likes pizza more? Grade seven, even though its count was smaller.
Here is a different question. Of the students who like pizza, what part are in grade seven?
Now we divide by the Likes pizza column total, twenty-seven.
So it is twelve out of twenty-seven, which simplifies to four ninths.
When the question asks about grade seven students, don't divide by all fifty students.
Divide by the Grade seven row total, twenty, and you get sixty percent.

Now you try. A mat is one and one half feet long and one and one half feet wide. Each small tile is one half foot on a side. How many square feet is the mat? Count the small tiles. Then change them to square feet.
Now you try. Is every rectangle a parallelogram? Think of the rule for the family. Does the shape follow it?
Now you try. Each cube is one cubic inch. What is the volume of this box in cubic inches? Count the cubes one layer at a time. Each cube is one cubic inch.
Now you try. How far across is point A? Go along the bottom first, until you are right under the point.
Now you try. Which point is at three, one? Go across first, then up. Which point is there?
Now you try. Pattern A, start at zero, add two. Pattern B, start at zero, add eight. What is the fifth number in pattern B? Start at zero. Follow the rule one step at a time.

Now you try. Pattern A, start at zero, add one. Pattern B, start at zero, add three. Pattern A goes across. When the dot is two across, how far up is it? Find the column. The bottom number tells how far up.
Now you try. Point A is at one comma four. Point B is at eight comma four. How many units apart are they? Find the number they share. Subtract the other two.
Now you try. On the map, the school is at two comma three and the pool is at two comma nine. How many blocks apart are they? Find the number they share. Subtract the other two.
Now you try. A bracelet pattern has four green beads for every three yellow beads. Green beads are four out of every how many beads? The whole means every bead in one set, both colors.
Now you try. A lemonade recipe uses two lemons for every five cups of water. How many cups of water go with six lemons? Find what the lemons were multiplied by. Do the same to the water.
Now you try. A pack of four pens costs seven dollars. How much does one pen cost? Split the total into one equal part for each pen.
Now you try. four movie tickets cost eighteen dollars. How much do six tickets cost? Find the price of one ticket first. Then multiply.

Now you try. A smoothie uses two cups of berries for every three cups of yogurt. How many cups of yogurt go with ten cups of berries? Use the columns you already have. Multiply one, or add two together.
Now you try. A club has three boys for every four girls. There are twenty-eight members. How many girls are in the club? Count all the boxes first. Then find what one box holds.
Now you try. A rug is five yards long. one yard is three feet. How many feet long is the rug? Start from one yard. Smaller units means more of them.
Now you try. A train goes one hundred fifty miles in three hours. How many miles does it go in one hour? Cut the trip into one equal jump for each hour.

Now you try. You have two thirds of a pan of cornbread. Each serving is one sixth of the pan. How many servings can you cut? Find two thirds divided by one sixth. Cut the shaded part into pieces the size of one serving. Then count them.

Now you try. You have three liters of juice. Each bottle holds three fourths liter. How many bottles can you fill? Find three divided by three fourths. Keep the first number, change divide to times, and flip the fraction you divide by.
Now you try. Find one and one half times two and one third. Change both mixed numbers into fractions. Then multiply.

Now you try. You have three and three fourths pounds of ground beef. Each patty uses three fourths pound. How many patties can you make? Change the mixed number into a fraction. Then flip and multiply.
Now you try. You have four yards of ribbon. Each bow uses two thirds yard. How many bows can you make? Start with the amount you have. Divide by the size of one bow.
Now you try. What is the biggest number that is a factor of both sixteen and twenty-four? List the factors of each number. Find the biggest one on both lists.
Now you try. What is the smallest number that is a multiple of both six and eight? Count by each number. Stop at the first number both counts reach.
Now you try. Take away. Fifteen point four minus six point two three seven equals what? Line up the points. Fill the empty places with zeros. Take away from the right.
Now you try. Multiply. Three point two times one point four equals what? Multiply without the points. Count the places. Put the point back.
Now you try. Divide. Nine point four five divided by three equals what? Put the point on top first. Then divide like whole numbers.
Now you try. Divide. Seven point two divided by zero point three equals what? Multiply both numbers by ten or one hundred until the outside number is whole. Then divide.
Now you try. Find four thousand three hundred sixty-eight divided by twenty-four. Guess each digit with a round number. Multiply, take away, bring down.
Now you try. Pens come three for two dollars and eighty-five cents or five for four dollars and sixty cents. Which is the better buy? Find the price of one pen in each pack. Pick the lower one.
Now you try. This grid has one hundred equal squares. What percent of the grid is shaded? Count the shaded squares. Out of one hundred, that count is the percent.
Now you try. What percent is one fourth? Make the fraction out of one hundred. Then read the percent.
Now you try. What is forty percent of seventy? Find ten percent first. Then take the parts you need.
Now you try. twelve is twenty-five percent of what number? Find how many equal pieces make one hundred percent. Then count them all.
Now you try. Shoes cost sixty dollars. They are twenty percent off. What is the sale price, in dollars? Find the money you save. Then take it away from the price.
Now you try. A jacket costs fifty dollars. The sales tax is six percent. What is the total, in dollars? Find the tax. Then add it to the price.

Now you try. You put six hundred dollars in a bank that pays three percent a year. How many dollars does the bank pay you in two years? Just what the bank pays, not the six hundred dollars. Find one year first. Then multiply by the years.

Now you try. A box holds n pencils. You also have four more pencils, so you have n plus four pencils. How many pencils is that when n equals six? Find what n stands for. Put that number where the n is.
Now you try. Which shows seven more than n? Find the action word. Then write it with n.
Now you try. What is two n plus five when n equals six? Put the number where the letter is. Then do the math.
Now you try. What is three cubed? Write the big number as many times as the small number says. Then multiply.
Now you try. What is five plus two times three squared? Parentheses, then exponents, then times and divide, then plus and minus.
Now you try. Which is the same as four times x plus three, all together? Multiply the number outside by every part inside.
Now you try. Solve x plus six equals fifteen. What is x? Take the same amount off both sides until x is alone.
Now you try. Solve four x equals twenty-eight. What is x? Divide both sides by the number in front of x.
Now you try. Which number line shows x is less than six? Decide the dot first, does the number itself work? Then decide which way the arrow goes.

Now you try. This shape has a base of seven centimeters and a height of four centimeters. Its slanted side is five centimeters. What is its area in square centimeters? Multiply the base by the straight-up height.
Now you try. A triangle has a base of eight centimeters and a height of five centimeters. What is its area in square centimeters? Multiply the base by the height. Then take half.

Now you try. A wall is a rectangle eight feet wide and five feet tall with a triangle roof three feet tall on top. What is its area in square feet? Cut it into a rectangle and a triangle. Find each area, then add.

Now you try. This box is five centimeters long, three centimeters wide and two centimeters tall. It is unfolded flat below. How many square centimeters of paper cover it? Find the area of every flat side, then add all six.
Now you try. A box is three and one half ft long, two feet wide and one and one half ft tall. What is its volume in cubic feet? Change the mixed numbers to fractions. Then multiply all three edges.

Now you try. Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. One is sixty-five degrees. How many degrees is the other? The angles on a straight line add up to one hundred eighty degrees. Take away the one you know.
Now you try. Four towers have three, seven, four and six cubes. If the cubes are shared fairly, how many cubes are in each tower? Add all the cubes. Then share the total into equal towers.
Now you try. Five seedlings are eight, two, five, nine and four inches tall. What is the middle height? Sort the heights first. Then find the one in the middle.
Now you try. twelve kids said how many brothers and sisters they have. Which number is the most common? Find the tallest stack. Read the number under it.
Now you try. Leo scored six, thirteen, eight, seventeen and ten points in five games. What is the biggest score minus the smallest score? Find the smallest and the biggest. Then subtract.
Now you try. Five kids get six dollars, five dollars, seven dollars, six dollars and thirty-six dollars a week. Which middle describes these amounts best? Look for a number far from the rest.
Now you try. Kids marked how many books they read this month. How many kids read three or more books? Find the stacks you need. Count their Xs and add.
Now you try. This spinner has eight equal parts. What is the chance of landing on blue? Ways it can happen on top. All the ways on the bottom.
Now you try. A bag has five marbles, one yellow and four purple. You pick one without looking. How likely is yellow? Find the chance as a fraction. Then see where it sits on the line.

Now you try. Tables with one steady rate are called proportional. The table shows the cost of movie tickets. Is it proportional? Divide each cost by its number of tickets. Are the answers all the same?
Now you try. A hose fills a tank at a steady rate. What number do you multiply the minutes by to get the gallons? Divide the gallons by the minutes. Check it with a second column.
Now you try. This graph is proportional. It goes through the points zero, zero and two, six. What is y when x equals one? Find x equals one on the bottom. Go up to the line and read y.
Now you try. You walk three fourths mile in one fourth hour. How many miles do you walk in one hour? Count how many of those time pieces make one whole hour.
Now you try. On a map, three inches stands for twenty miles. Two towns are twelve inches apart. How many miles apart are they? Find what the inches were multiplied by. Do the same to the miles.
Now you try. A game cost forty dollars. Now it costs forty-six dollars. By what percent did the price go up? Find the change. Divide it by the original price, then multiply by one hundred.
Now you try. A shop pays thirty dollars for a hat and adds forty percent on top. What is the price, in dollars? Find forty percent of what the shop paid. Then add it on.
Now you try. You guess a jar holds sixty-eight marbles. The real count is eighty. By what percent was your guess off? Find the gap. Divide it by the real count, then multiply by one hundred.
Now you try. What is the opposite of negative six? Count the steps from zero. Go the same distance on the other side.
Now you try. How far is negative eight from zero? Count the steps from the number to zero. Drop the sign.
Now you try. Add. four plus negative seven equals what? Pair each plus with a minus. Take the pairs away. Count what is left.
Now you try. Take away. negative one minus six equals what? Change minus to plus and use the opposite. Then move on the line.
Now you try. Multiply. Negative four times negative three equals what? Multiply without the signs. Then check, same signs or different?
Now you try. Divide. Negative twenty divided by negative five equals what? Divide without the signs. Then check, same signs or different?
Now you try. Add. Negative one fourth plus three fourths equals what? Keep the minus sign. Start at the first number and jump on the line.

Now you try. It is negative four degrees Celsius in the morning. By the afternoon it is nine degrees warmer. What is the temperature in the afternoon, in degrees Celsius? Let the words pick the sign. Then climb the thermometer.
Now you try. Which is the same as four x plus two plus three x plus six? Put the x parts together. Then put the plain numbers together.
Now you try. Which is the same as negative three times x minus five, all together? Multiply the number outside by every part inside. Watch the signs.
Now you try. Which is the same as eight x plus twelve? Find the biggest number that divides every part. Put it outside.
Now you try. Solve three x plus five equals twenty. What is x? Undo the adding first. Then undo the multiplying.
Now you try. Solve four times x plus three, all together, equals thirty-two. What is x? Divide both sides by the number outside. Then solve what is left.
Now you try. Solve three x plus two is greater than fourteen. Which is the answer? Solve it like an equation. Keep the sign.
Now you try. Solve negative two x is less than ten. Which is the answer? Divide both sides. If you divide by a negative, flip the sign.

Now you try. A gym costs fifteen dollars to join, plus eight dollars for each class. Leo paid sixty-three dollars. How many classes did he take? Use a letter for what you do not know. Write the equation, then solve it.

Now you try. On a map, one centimeter equals fifty meters. A road is eight centimeters long on the map. How many meters long is the real road? Find what one centimeter stands for. Then multiply by the map length.
Now you try. A plate has a diameter of twenty centimeters. How far is it around the edge, in centimeters? Use three point one four. Multiply the distance across by three point one four.
Now you try. A round rug has a radius of three meters. What is its area in square meters? Use pi as three point one four. Multiply the radius by itself. Then multiply by three point one four.
Now you try. Two angles make a square corner. One is twenty-eight degrees. How many degrees is the other? Find the whole first. Then take away the angle you know.
Now you try. Two straight lines cross. One angle is sixty-five degrees. What is the angle straight across from it? Is the missing angle straight across, or next door?
Now you try. Can sticks two centimeters, five centimeters and eight centimeters long make a triangle? Add the two shorter sides. Is that more than the longest?

Now you try. A wedge has triangle ends with sides three centimeters, four centimeters and five centimeters, and it is eight centimeters long. It is unfolded flat below. What is the area of all its faces in square centimeters? Find the area of both ends and all three sides. Then add.
Now you try. A box is six centimeters long, three centimeters wide and four centimeters tall. What is its volume in cubic centimeters? Find the area of the base. Then multiply by the height.

Now you try. You want to know how students at your school get to school. You ask the first twenty kids who get off one bus. Is that a fair sample? Ask, does everyone in the school have the same chance to be picked?

Now you try. You ask forty students, picked by chance. ten of them walk to school. Predict how many of all six hundred students walk to school. Find the fraction in the sample. Then take that fraction of the whole school.
Now you try. Two classes each grew five plants. What is the difference between their mean heights, in inches? Find the mean of each class. Then subtract.
Now you try. This spinner has ten equal parts. What is the probability of landing on green? Write a fraction or a decimal. Ways it can happen on top. All the equal ways on the bottom.
Now you try. You roll a number cube sixty times. How many times do you expect to roll a four? Find the chance on one roll. Multiply it by the number of rolls.
Now you try. You flip a coin and roll a number cube. What is the probability of tails and an even number? Fill in the table. Count the pairs you want over all the pairs.
Now you try. Write three to the fourth times three squared as three with one exponent. What is the exponent? Keep the base. Add the exponents.
Now you try. Write three to the seventh divided by three squared as three with one exponent. What is the exponent? Keep the base. Subtract the bottom exponent from the top one.
Now you try. Write three squared, all to the fourth, as three with one exponent. What is the exponent? Keep the base. Multiply the exponents.
Now you try. What is three to the negative two? Write it as a fraction. Start from a value you know. Divide by the base for each step down.
Now you try. four million five hundred thousand equals four point five times ten to some power. What is the exponent? Make a number from one up to ten. Count how many places the point jumps.
Now you try. Zero point zero zero zero seven equals seven times ten to the what? What is the exponent? Move the point right to make a number from one up to ten. Count the jumps, and make it negative.
Now you try. three times ten to the fifth, times three times ten squared, equals nine times ten to the what? What is the exponent? Multiply the front numbers. Add the exponents of ten.
Now you try. What is the square root of forty-nine? Find the number that times itself makes forty-nine.
Now you try. Between which two whole numbers is the square root of fifty? Find the perfect square just below fifty and the one just above.
Now you try. The line goes through the points two, one and four, seven. How steep is it? Find rise divided by run. Count across, then up. Divide the up by the across.
Now you try. A line goes through the points one, four and five, sixteen. What is its slope? Subtract the y-values, then the x-values in the same order. Divide.
Now you try. A line has the equation y equals three x plus five. What is its slope? Find the number in front of x.
Now you try. Which point is on the line y equals two x minus one? Put each point’s x into the equation. Does it give that point’s y?
Now you try. Solve six x plus five equals three x plus twenty. What is x? Take the smaller x part off both sides. Then solve what is left.
Now you try. How many solutions does four x plus one equals four x plus seven have? Take the x parts off both sides. Look at what is left.
Now you try. The lines y equals x plus one and y equals negative x plus seven cross at one point. What is the x-value of that point? Find where the lines meet. Check the point in both equations.
Now you try. y equals three x and x plus y equals sixteen. What is x? Put what y equals in place of y. Then solve for x.

Now you try. A family buys nine tickets. Adult tickets cost six dollars and kid tickets cost three dollars. They pay thirty-nine dollars. How many adult tickets did they buy? Write one equation for the tickets and one for the dollars. Then solve them together.
Now you try. Is this table a function? Look along the input row. Does any input show up twice with a different output?
Now you try. The rule is output equals three times input minus two. What is the output when the input is six? Put the input into the rule. Multiply first, then subtract.
Now you try. Is this table linear? Check that x goes up in equal steps. Then find how much y changes each step.
Now you try. Function A is the table. Function B is y equals three x plus ten. Which grows faster? Find how much each one goes up for each one in x. Compare the two numbers.
Now you try. A skating rink costs fifteen dollars to join, plus eight dollars for each visit. Which rule gives the cost y for x visits? Find the amount that repeats and the amount paid once.

Now you try. The graph shows how many miles Mia is from home. Along the bottom is hours. What is her distance doing between hour three and hour five? Find the two hours along the bottom. Is that piece going up, going down or flat?
Now you try. Point A is at two, one. The triangle slides five right and three up. What is the x-coordinate of A prime? Right and left change x. Up and down change y.
Now you try. Point A is at three, two. The triangle flips over the x-axis. What is the y-coordinate of A prime? Over the x-axis, the y changes sign. Over the y-axis, the x changes sign.

Now you try. Point A is at four, two. The triangle turns a quarter turn counterclockwise around the point zero, zero. What is the x-coordinate of A prime? Swap the two numbers. Then change the sign of the new first number.
Now you try. Point A is at three, one. The triangle is stretched from the point zero, zero, multiplying by two. What is the x-coordinate of A prime? Multiply both coordinates by the stretch number.

Now you try. These two triangles have the same angles. The small one has sides six, five and three centimeters. The big one has sides eighteen, fifteen and ? cm. How long is the missing side, in cm? Find the scale factor from a matching pair. Then multiply.
Now you try. A triangle has angles of forty degrees and seventy-five degrees. What is the third angle, in degrees? Add the two angles you know. Take that away from one hundred eighty degrees.
Now you try. A right triangle has short sides of six centimeters and eight centimeters. How long is the long side, in cm? Square the two short sides, add, then undo the square.

Now you try. A right triangle has a long side of ten centimeters and a short side of six centimeters. How long is the other short side, in cm? Square the long side, take away the square of the short side, then undo the square.
Now you try. How far apart are the points two, one and eight, nine, in units? Find how far across and how far up. Those are the legs.

Now you try. A can has a radius of two inches and a height of seven inches. What is its volume in cubic inches? Use pi as three point one four. Find the area of the circle. Then multiply by the height.

Now you try. A cone has a radius of three centimeters and a height of five centimeters. What is its volume in cubic centimeters? Use pi as three point one four. Find the cylinder with the same bottom and height. Then divide by three.

Now you try. A ball has a radius of six centimeters. What is its volume in cubic centimeters? Use pi as three point one four. Multiply the radius by itself three times. Take four thirds of that, then multiply by three point one four.

Now you try. An ice-cream cone has a radius of three centimeters and a height of eight centimeters. Half a ball of ice cream with a radius of three centimeters sits on top. How many cubic centimeters is that in all? Use pi as three point one four. Name the two shapes. Find each one, then add.
Now you try. Each dot is one day at a cafe, the temperature and the cups of hot chocolate sold. What pattern does the plot show? Look at the whole cloud. Does it rise, fall, or neither?
Now you try. A line fits these dots well. It passes through the point zero, forty and the point five, seventy. What is its slope? Find the rise and the run between the two points. Then divide.
Now you try. The line of best fit for hours studied and test score is y equals five x plus fifty. Predict the score for eight hours of studying. Put the hours in place of x. Multiply, then add.
Now you try. How many grade seven students do not like pizza? Find the row the box is in. Its boxes add up to its total.
Now you try. What percent of grade seven students like pizza? Ask out of whom? Divide the count by that total, then write it as a percent.
How many plates are there? How many cookies are on each plate?
There are three groups of five. Count by fives, one plate at a time. five, ten, and keep going.
How many groups are there? How many are in each group?
sources: g3m1-t1 twin hint1 + g3m1-t2 twin hint1 + g3m1-t4 twin hint1 + g3m1-t5 twin hint1

text: There are five groups of two. Count by twos. two, four, and keep going.
How many rows are there? How many plants are in one row?
There are four rows of three. Count by threes, one row at a time. three, six, and keep going.
There are two groups of five. Count by fives. five, and keep going.
Tap turn. Were any dots added or taken away?
ten times four is the same dots turned around, so it has the same total as four times ten.
Turn the rows around. Were any added or taken away?
five times three is the same rows as three times five, turned around.
Count by fives. Hold up one finger for each hand you count.
five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty is six hands. Make one more jump.
There are six groups of ten. Count by tens. ten, twenty, and keep going.
Each car has four wheels. Jump by fours, one jump for each car.
four, eight, twelve, sixteen is four cars. Make one more jump.
There are six groups of three. Count by threes, three, six, and so on.
Give one cookie to each friend. Then go round again until none are left.
After four rounds, each plate has four cookies and two are left. Give one more to each friend.
Give one to each group. Then go round again until none are left.
Share fifteen into five equal groups. How many does each group get?
Ring five stickers to make one pack. Keep going until none are left.
two packs of five use ten stickers. five are left. That makes one more pack.
Make a group of four. Keep going until none are left.
Count by fours until you reach twenty, four, eight, and so on. How many groups?
three groups of what number make thirty?
Count by tens three times, ten, twenty, thirty. What did you count by?
five times what number makes fifteen?
Count by fives until you reach fifteen. How many jumps did you make?
Which number is the short hand just past?
The long hand is on the five. Count by fives five times.
The long hand is on the eight. Count by fives eight times.
Which number has the long hand just passed?
Count by fives to the three. Then count the little marks one at a time.
Count by fives to the seven. Then count the little marks one at a time.
Start at one fifteen. Jump to the next ten first.
From one twenty, jump by tens to one forty. Then add all your jumps.
Start at twelve oh five. Jump five minutes to the next ten.
From twelve ten, jump by tens to twelve fifty. Then add all your jumps.
How much is each little mark worth?
sources: g3m2-t4 hint1 + g3m2-t4 twin hint1 + g3m2-t5 hint1 + g3m2-t5 twin hint1

text: Each mark is one hundred grams. Find the number just before the needle and count on.
Each mark is one kilogram. Find the number just before the needle and count on.
Each mark is one hundred milliliters. Find the number just below the water and count up.
Each mark is one liter. Find the number just below the water and count up.
Which two tens is sixty-two between?
sixty-two is two jumps from one ten and eight jumps from the other. Which is closer?
Which two tens is seventy-eight between?
seventy-eight is eight jumps from one ten and two jumps from the other. Which is closer?
Which two hundreds is four hundred twenty between?
four hundred twenty is two jumps of ten from one hundred and eight jumps from the other. Which is closer?
Which two hundreds is six hundred eighty between?
six hundred eighty is eight jumps of ten from one hundred and two jumps from the other. Which is closer?
Add the ones first. Is it ten or more?
five plus seven equals twelve. Write the two and trade ten ones for one ten.
six plus nine equals fifteen. Write the five and trade ten ones for one ten.
Look at the ones. Can you take eight from three?
Break one ten into ten ones. Now there are thirteen ones and five tens.
Look at the ones. Can you take six from two?
Break one ten into ten ones. Now there are twelve ones and six tens.
How many cookies are on each plate?
Each plate adds zero cookies. What do you get when you add zero six times?
Look at one plate. How many cookies does it add?
Each of the nine plates adds zero. What do you get when you add zero nine times?
Each plate has just one cookie. So count the plates.
How many plates are there? How many cookies are on the plate?
There is only one plate. Count the cookies on it.
Find five rows of four first. What is five times four?
five times four equals twenty. Now add one more row of four.
Find five rows of five first. What is five times five?
five times five equals twenty-five. Now add one more row of five.
Break the seven rows into five rows and two rows.
sources: g3m3-t4 hint1 + g3m3-t4 twin hint1 + g3m3-t7 hint1

text: five times four equals twenty and two times four equals eight. Now add them.
five times five equals twenty-five and two times five equals ten. Now add them.
Find four packs of four first. What is four times four?
four times four equals sixteen. Now double it.
Find four packs of five first. What is four times five?
four times five equals twenty. Now double it.
Find ten boxes of four first. What is ten times four?
ten times four equals forty. Now take away one box of four.
Find ten boxes of six first. What is ten times six?
ten times six equals sixty. Now take away one box of six.
five times nine equals forty-five and two times nine equals eighteen. Now add the parts.
Break the eight rows into five rows and three rows.
five times six equals thirty and three times six equals eighteen. Now add the parts.
How many tens are in fifty? Multiply the tens.
three times five equals fifteen. So it is fifteen tens. How many straws is that?
How many tens are in twenty? Multiply the tens.
four times two equals eight. So it is eight tens. How many straws is that?
First find how many stickers Mia buys. Then take away the ones she uses.
four times six equals twenty-four. Now take away nine.
First find how many crayons Leo buys. Then take away the ones he loses.
five times eight equals forty. Now take away six.
Count each tile once. Try going across one row at a time.
The top row has five tiles. Keep counting along every row.
Count every tile once. Do not skip any.
Count the top row. Then keep counting along the bottom row.
How many rows are there? How many tiles are in one row?
There are four rows of six. Count by sixes, one row at a time. six, twelve, and keep going.
There are two rows of five. Count by fives, one row at a time.
What is the area of each piece? Then add them.
The pieces are three times five and three times three. Find each one, then add.
Find the area of each piece. Then add the two areas.
The pieces are four times five and four times two. Find each one, then add.
Cut the room into two rectangles. Find the area of each one.
The tall part is four rows of three. The short part is two rows of three. Add their areas.
The tall part is five rows of two. The short part is two rows of three. Add their areas.
Are all the pieces the same size?
Compare the middle piece with the pieces at the ends.
Look at each piece. Do they all match?
Put your finger on each piece and compare it with the next one.
How many equal pieces is the whole bar cut into?
The shaded piece is one of those pieces. Put the one on top.
How many equal pieces is the strip cut into?
You ate one piece. That number goes on top.
How many equal pieces make the whole bar? That is the bottom.
Now count only the shaded pieces. That is the top.
How many equal pieces is the whole pan cut into?
Count only the shaded pieces. That number goes on top.
How many equal jumps go from zero to one?
Start at zero and count the jumps until you reach the dot.
Start at zero. Count the jumps to the dot. The zero is where you start, not a jump.
Look at where the shading stops on each bar.
Each piece on the top bar was cut into two smaller pieces. Did the shaded amount change?
Each piece on the top bar sits over how many small pieces below?
Look under the shaded piece on top. Count the small pieces under it.
How many equal pieces are in the whole bar?
Count the shaded pieces. Are any pieces white?
How many equal pieces is the sandwich cut into?
The whole sandwich means every piece. Count them all.
Are the bottom numbers the same?
Shade two pieces on one bar and five on the other in your head. Which covers more?
Are the pieces the same size?
Compare the top numbers. Which one has more pieces?
Both take the same number of pieces. Which bar has bigger pieces?
Fewer cuts make bigger pieces. Which bar has fewer cuts?
